title: Numbers, numbers, numbers - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Cowen uses Munich Re and Aon market data on the cyber-insurance market (~$15B growing to ~$28B by 2030, ~20% of attacks involving generative AI by 2027) plus a Claude 5.1 estimate of $100-300B in current U.S. cybersecurity costs to argue cyber/AI-driven security costs are rising roughly 13%/year — serious but not civilization-ending.

themes.theme: Quantifying AI-driven cyber risk via market data

insights.claim: Munich Re estimates the global cyber insurance market was worth nearly $15 billion in 2025 and is expected to reach roughly $28 billion by 2030, implying growth close to a doubling over five years.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A near-doubling of the global cyber insurance market by 2030 is a direct growth signal for insurers and reinsurers underwriting cyber risk, and an implied proxy for rising aggregate cyber-loss exposure.
insights.quote: The global cyber insurance market was worth nearly $15 billion last year and is expected to reach roughly $28 billion by 2030, Munich Re estimated in its latest report.

insights.claim: Aon forecasts that nearly 20% of cyberattacks will involve generative AI by 2027.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A concrete, sourced forecast for how quickly generative AI is expected to penetrate the attack landscape, useful for sizing AI-driven cybersecurity demand and vendor opportunity (e.g., AI-native security firms).
insights.quote: Aon said earlier this year that nearly 20% of cyberattacks will involve generative AI by 2027, according to its forecasts.

insights.claim: Cowen cites a Claude 5.1 estimate that current U.S. cybersecurity costs run in the range of $100 to $300 billion, and reasons this could roughly double over five years given the trajectory implied by the cyber-insurance market growth.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A rough but sourced order-of-magnitude estimate for total U.S. cybersecurity spend that investors can use as a sizing anchor for the cybersecurity sector's addressable market growth.
insights.quote: Claude 5.1 for instances estimates current U.S. cybersecurity costs in the range of $100 to $300 billion, and of course that is slated to go up a fair amount.

insights.claim: Cowen frames the implied trajectory as cyber costs rising roughly thirteen percent a year, offering both an optimistic read (defense spending eventually catches up to the threat) and a pessimistic read (costs compound at 13%/year until the economy is meaningfully strained).
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A simple compounding-growth heuristic (13%/year) for framing how fast cyber/AI security costs could scale, useful as a baseline assumption when modeling cybersecurity sector TAM or enterprise IT cost inflation.
insights.quote: One way of looking at that estimate is to think that cyber costs will go up about thirteen percent a year, and eventually defense will catch up.

insights.claim: Cowen's broader methodological point is that market-and-industry-sourced numbers (even imperfect, sectoral ones) are more useful for reasoning about AI-driven cyber risk than qualitative anecdotes or alarmist narratives.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A recurring Cowen framework across his AI-risk posts this period: push commentators toward quantifiable, market-anchored estimates rather than narrative-driven doom framing when assessing AI risk.
insights.quote: I am not saying the numbers above are the right numbers, but I am saying they are better than no numbers at all.
